newsitem.title: INDIA: India gets budget for growth, must keep promises.
newsitem.headline: India gets budget for growth, must keep promises.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram delivered a budget on Friday to woo investors and drive growth, but skeptics wondered whether he could keep promised reforms moving.
Stock markets gave an immediate thumbs up to Chidambaram's sweeping cuts in personal and corporate taxes in a budget that aimed to keep economic growth and liberalisation on track.
The Bombay Stock Exchange leapt 5.13 percent, or 178.2 points, to a provisional close of 3,652.99 at the end of a special post-budget evening session.

A decision to allow foreign institutions to raise their holdings in Indian firms to 30 percent from a current limit of 24 percent gave a boost, as investors poured into favourites State Bank of India and Reliance Industries.

"This is the first time that so much has been done for investors in one budget," Madan Gopal Damani, president of the Bombay Stock Exchange said, adding: "It is a bright future for industrial growth because of vibrant capital markets."
But his counterpart at the rival National Stock Exchange saw some grounds for worry.

"The fiscal deficit figures are a puzzle to me given all these concessions on the revenue front. I don't know whether he is assuming a big spurt in revenue," R.H. Patil, managing director of the National Stock Exchange, told Reuters.
Chidambaram pegged the fiscal defict at 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997/98, down from a targeted 5.0 percent in 1996/97.
The finance minister is gambling that by widening the tax net and improving collection he can offset a loss in revenues from the cut in tax rates.
But Patil was confident measures to attract portfolio investment would pay off. He said that in 1996/97, foreign institutional investors poured $3 billion into the economy.
"This year we should see a 30 percent spurt to at least $4 billion," he said.

Analysts were disappointed Chidamabaram had not done more to generate confidence for foreign investors in India's ailing infrastruture, which is seen as a key constraint on economic growth. India is aiming to attract $10 billion of foreign direct investment annually for the next few years.

"It is a very market-friendly budget but has not done enough for infrastructure or industrial growth. The market may rally, but I see it tapering off in six months," said Dinshaw Irani, head of research at Lloyds Securities Ltd in Bombay. "As of now he has kick-started the economy, but what we need is growth."
If the bull run in stock prices keeps going -- and most analysts believe it can stay intact for some months at least -- Chidamabaram will have achieved one of his key aims.

The finance minister needed to come up with a budget to convince speculators to keep faith with India in order to prime markets for heavy government divestment of its stakes in state-controlled companies.

Chidambaram plans to raise 48 billion rupees ($1.3 billion) through selloffs in 1997/98. It wants to put Gas Authority of India Ltd, Modern Food Industries Ltd (India) and India Tourism Development Corp on the frontline of the divestment programme.
The state expects to raise just five billion rupees of a targeted 50 billion through divestments in 1996/97 after adverse market conditions stalled several launches.
That failure to deliver has been symptomatic of the 15-party coalition government, and has left investors jaundiced about its ability to carry through reforms.
"The disappointment is that many promises are not fulfilled and fresh ones are given," said Dinesh Vyas, a Supreme Court advocate and a member of India's central board of direct taxes.
"All these promises build up a rosy picture. But the real test of the budget lies in how far these will be implemented." ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
